title: Sunset Blvd: One Famous Road
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with an iHeart intro voice) tour Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles, from its origins as a cattle trail and the Pueblo de Los Angeles through its film-studio, Prohibition-era vice, hotel, nightclub, rock, comedy and hair metal history. Topics include Sunset Gower Studios and Gower Gulch, the Sunset Strip's mob clubs and brothels, the Chateau Marmont, Garden of Allah, Schwab's Pharmacy, the Whiskey a Go Go, the 1966 Sunset Strip riots, the Black Cat Tavern protest, the Roxy, Rodney's English Disco, the Comedy Store and Laugh Factory, and the Rainbow Bar and Grill. The episode ends with listener mail from Austin about playing rock paper scissors with three or more people.

segments.title: Opening banter and Sunset Boulevard origins
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode and discuss Sunset Boulevard's history, from its start as a cattle trail from the Pueblo de Los Angeles to the Pacific and the naming of the street.

segments.title: Hollywood geography and early film studios
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Hollywood basin and neighborhoods along the street, then the early film studios at Sunset and Gower, now Sunset Gower Studios.

segments.title: Gower Gulch and the Columbia Drug Store
segments.summary: Westerns were filmed around Gower and cowboy extras gathered at Gower Gulch and the Columbia Drug Store, which had a phone extras used to call Central Casting. A shooting between cowboys is recounted.

segments.title: Prohibition-era Sunset Strip and mob clubs
segments.summary: During Prohibition the unincorporated County Strip had mobster clubs, gambling and nightclubs under weak county enforcement, and was popular with movie stars from Beverly Hills. Mob-owned clubs included the Sphinx, the Hane Club, Socoloff's and the Clover Club, now a dispensary.

segments.title: Hollywood brothels and celebrity madams
segments.summary: The hosts discuss brothels along Sunset, rumored lookalike sex workers tied to L.A. Confidential, and madams Leah Francis and Black Widow Forrester, whose client records disappeared and whose cases led to no arrests.

segments.title: Gay bars, Trocadero and Ciro's
segments.summary: West Hollywood's early gay and drag clubs, including Café Lobo, and the Trocadero opened by Billy Wilkerson in 1934. Ciro's nightclub is noted for Bugsy Siegel having food delivered to jail.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break.

segments.title: Chateau Marmont discretion
segments.summary: The Chateau Marmont, built in 1929, kept its guests' privacy through strict staff discretion. Harry Cohn reportedly told actors to get in trouble there. Hosts mention its John Belushi Bungalow and its reopening as a hotel.

segments.title: Garden of Allah and Schwab's Pharmacy
segments.summary: Alla Nazimova's Garden of Allah house-turned-hotel was a safe social space for queer actresses. Across the street, Schwab's Pharmacy was a gathering place for hopefuls and stars, and the Lana Turner discovery story is corrected to the Top Hat malt shop.

segments.title: Sunset Strip becomes rock scene; Whisky a Go Go
segments.summary: Lower rents after Vegas drew performers led to grittier clubs and Black performers playing the strip. Rock clubs followed, and the Whisky a Go Go opened in 1964, with Joni Mitchell's DJ booth popularizing go-go dancing.

segments.title: Doors, cruising and American Graffiti
segments.summary: The Whisky was the house band venue for the Doors in 1966. Cruising the strip became popular in the mid-1960s, and the hosts discuss American Graffiti and its alternate title Burger City.

segments.title: 1966 Sunset Strip riot and Pandora's Box
segments.summary: A curfew for teenagers led to a November 1966 protest in front of Pandora's Box, which ended with police violence. Stephen Stills wrote For What It's Worth after witnessing it.

segments.title: Black Cat Tavern protest
segments.summary: Police raids on the gay Black Cat Tavern on New Year's Eve led to beatings, arrests, and a February 1967 protest described as the first recorded LGBTQ protest in US history. The bar lost its liquor license. The Silver Lake Black Cat restaurant reopened later. A brief Shake Shack anecdote is included.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Sponsor break.

segments.title: Seventies rock clubs and Van Halen
segments.summary: The Roxy, Rodney's English Disco and Ghazarian's were key seventies rock clubs. Van Halen played house gigs at Ghazarian's. The hosts discuss Eddie Van Halen's comments about Michael Anthony and Sammy Hagar's response.

segments.title: Roxy, Rodney's English Disco and Rodney Bingenheimer
segments.summary: The Roxy opened in 1973 and staged early US Rocky Horror and Pee-wee Herman shows. Rodney's English Disco opened in 1972. Rodney Bingenheimer's sexual assault allegations are discussed.

segments.title: Riot House and Rainbow Bar and Grill
segments.summary: The Continental Hyatt House, originally the Continental owned by Gene Autry, was known as the Riot House. The Rainbow Bar and Grill was the Hollywood Vampires hangout, and John Belushi ate his last meal there.

segments.title: Comedy Store, Laugh Factory and comedy strikes
segments.summary: Mitzi Shore's Comedy Store opened in 1972 as a stand-up workshop, with unpaid comics who later went on strike. The Laugh Factory opened in 1979 and paid comics a share of the cover charge.

segments.title: Eighties hair metal and Beverly Hills Hotel
segments.summary: Motley Crue and other hair metal bands played the Sunset Strip in the 1980s. The hosts mention Judas Priest's Parking Lot documentary and the Beverly Hills Hotel's Martinique banana leaf wallpaper.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts mention topics not covered, such as Hollywood High School and the Crossroads of the World, and thank Dave.

segments.title: Listener mail: rock paper scissors with three or more
segments.summary: Austin from St. Louis describes how landscapers played multi-person rock paper scissors as a knockout game.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Credits and the iHeartRadio sign-off.
